objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how each flight instrument shows pitch, bank and power, cross-check them without fixating, and hold straight-and-level flight by instruments alone within ACS limits.
why: VFR pilots who lose the horizon and have not trained on instruments lose control in about 10 minutes [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. Holding the wings level and the altitude steady on instruments is the skill that keeps you alive until you get out of the cloud.

prereading.what: Control and performance, primary and supporting instruments, trim, cross-check patterns and scan errors, interpretation.
prereading.label: IFH Ch 6, 6-1 to 6-14

prereading.what: Straight-and-level flight: pitch, bank, power and trim control, common errors.
prereading.label: IFH Ch 7, 7-1 to 7-13

prereading.what: Attitude indicator, heading indicator and turn coordinator: how they work and their errors.
prereading.label: IFH 5-19 to 5-21

prereading.what: Inadvertent VFR flight into IMC: recognition, control, getting help.
prereading.label: AFH 18-17 to 18-21

prereading.what: Spatial disorientation and how to cope with it.
prereading.label: PHAK 17-6 to 17-9

warmup: Close your eyes in a car on a long curved highway ramp. After a few seconds, can you tell if you are still turning? What does that tell you about flying in a cloud?

key_terms.def: Controlling the airplane's position in space by instruments instead of outside references [[23:134|IFH 6-1]].
Show attitude and power right away: the attitude indicator and power gauges (manifold pressure, tachometer) [[23:135|IFH 6-2]].
Show what the airplane is actually doing: altimeter, airspeed indicator, VSI [[23:135|IFH 6-2]].
The one that gives the most useful information for the maneuver; usually the one you hold constant [[23:167|IFH 7-6]].
The continuous, logical look at the instruments for attitude and performance information [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].
The thickness of the miniature airplane's wings on the attitude indicator [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. The wings and center dot stand for about 2° of pitch [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].
3° per second, a full 360° in 2 minutes [[23:116|IFH 5-21]].
Losing track of the airplane's position, attitude or movement in space [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]].

body.p: Performance = attitude + power. You set an attitude and a power on the control instruments, then check the performance instruments to see if you got what you wanted [[23:135|IFH 6-2]].

bullets: 1. Set attitude and power for the performance you want.
2. Trim until control pressures are gone.
3. Cross-check the performance instruments.
4. Adjust attitude or power as needed.

body.p: The other method, primary and supporting, names the one instrument that tells you the most for pitch, bank and power. For straight-and-level at constant airspeed [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]:
From [[23:170|IFH 7-9]] and Figure 7-22.

callout.text: Level flight: Altimeter = pitch. Heading = bank. Airspeed = power.

body.p: "Primary" doesn't make the attitude indicator less important. It is the only instrument that shows the real attitude instantly and directly, so always use it when you have it [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].

check.q: In straight-and-level flight, which instrument is primary for bank?

body.p: At a given airspeed there is only one pitch attitude for level flight. Slow cruise is a bit nose-high; fast cruise is a bit nose-low [[23:163|IFH 7-2]]. Four instruments show pitch [[23:163|IFH 7-2]]:

head: Instrument
How it shows pitch
What to remember
rows: Directly: miniature airplane vs. horizon bar
Pitch changes on instruments are much smaller than in visual flight [[23:164|IFH 7-3]]
Indirectly: at constant power, altitude change means a pitch change
Fast needle = big pitch error; slow needle = small one [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]
Indirectly: shows the trend first, then the rate
Has lag; don't chase it in turbulence [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]
Indirectly: nose down, speed up; nose up, speed down
No real lag from the instrument itself [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]

body.p: Rules of thumb for getting back to altitude:

bullets: Error under 100 ft: half a bar width of pitch. Over 100 ft: start with a full bar width [[23:165|IFH 7-4]].
Pick a VSI rate about double the error: 100 ft off means about 200 fpm back [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].
More than 200 fpm away from the rate you wanted is overcontrolling [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].
Correct in two steps: first stop the needle, then return to altitude [[23:165|IFH 7-4]].

callout.text: Relax your grip. A tight grip hides control pressures. When trimmed, briefly let go: the airplane is stable and holds level flight if left alone, except in turbulence [[23:164|IFH 7-3]].

check.q: You are 150 ft high. How much pitch change do you start with?
check.a: A full bar width nose-down, since the error is over 100 ft [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]. Aim for about 300 fpm down (double the error) [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

body.p: Bank instruments are the attitude indicator, heading indicator and turn coordinator [[23:167|IFH 7-6]].

bullets: Attitude indicator: shows bank directly and instantly [[23:167|IFH 7-6]].
Heading indicator: shows bank indirectly. A fast-moving card means a big bank [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].
Turn coordinator: shows roll rate while rolling, then turn rate. The marks mean 3° per second [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

callout.text: Heading off? Bank no more degrees than you need to turn, and never more than standard rate [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

body.p: The ball shows the quality of the turn. Off center means a slip or skid. Center it with rudder on the side the ball is on (left ball, left rudder), level the wings with aileron, then retrim [[23:169|IFH 7-8]].

Power: at a given airspeed, power decides climb, level or descent. At a constant altitude, power decides airspeed [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]. Altitude and airspeed trade back and forth, so check the altimeter before changing power [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]:

head: You see
Fix
rows: Altitude high, airspeed low (or the reverse)
Pitch change alone may fix both [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]

body.p: Adding power makes the nose rise and the airplane yaw and roll left unless you hold forward pressure and counter with aileron and rudder [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].

check.q: Airspeed is 10 knots low and you're 100 ft high. Power or pitch?
check.a: Pitch: lower the nose to trade the extra altitude for airspeed [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].

body.p: Every instrument can lie a little. Know how each one fails so you catch it in your cross-check.

head: Instrument
Limit or error
Source
rows: Slight nose-up in rapid acceleration, nose-down in rapid deceleration; small bank and pitch error after a 180° turn. Fixes itself within a minute or so of straight-and-level.
Needs 2 to 3 minutes (up to 5) to erect after start. Older ones tumble past about 60° pitch or 100° roll.
Not north-seeking; drifts with Earth's rotation (15° per hour). Check it against the compass at least every 15 minutes.
Affected by turbulence, climbs, descents, power and speed changes; leads and lags in turns.
Lags a few seconds. Big, abrupt pitch changes give erratic or reversed readings.
May read a climb or descent while level. If so, use that reading as zero.
On the ground, set the altimeter setting; if it's off more than 75 ft from field elevation, get it fixed.

body.p: Errors in the airspeed indicator and VSI almost always mean a blocked pitot tube, static port, or both. Ice, water, dirt or insects can do it [[23:97|IFH 5-2]].

head: Blockage
What you see
rows: Pitot tube blocked, drain hole open
Pitot tube and drain hole blocked
Airspeed indicator acts like an altimeter [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]
Altimeter freezes; VSI stays at zero; airspeed reads low above that altitude, high below it [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]
Altimeter a bit high, airspeed a bit high, VSI shows a brief climb [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]

callout.text: On preflight, remove the pitot cover and look at the static ports [[23:97|IFH 5-2]]. Know what powers each gyro (vacuum or electric) from the POH so you know what fails together [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

check.q: Altimeter stuck, VSI on zero, but you know you're climbing. What failed?
check.a: A blocked static system [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]. Try the alternate static source if you have one.

body.p: No single scan pattern is required. Look at the instruments that give the best information for what you are doing [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]. Three common patterns [[23:144|IFH 6-11]]:

bullets: Radial: 80 to 90 percent of the time on the attitude indicator, with quick glances out to the others and back.
Inverted-V: attitude indicator, down to turn coordinator, back up, down to VSI, back up.
Rectangular: across the top row, then the bottom row. Equal weight to all, but slow to get back to the key one.

body.p: Three scan errors [[23:144|IFH 6-11]] [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]:

head: Error
What it looks like
rows: Staring at one instrument. You stare at an altimeter 200 ft low, tense up, and the heading wanders.
Leaving one out, like forgetting the heading indicator after rolling out of a turn.
Trusting the one you understand best. The attitude indicator alone can't hold altitude precisely; you need the altimeter.

body.p: Instrument interpretation means knowing what each reading says about attitude. Pitch comes from airspeed, altimeter, VSI and attitude indicator. Bank comes from heading indicator, turn coordinator and attitude indicator [[23:147|IFH 6-14]].

Trim: first hold the attitude with control pressure, then trim the pressure away. Center the ball with rudder trim if you have it [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]. Use trim often and in small amounts [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

callout.text: Don't fly with the trim wheel. Using trim alone to change attitude leads to erratic control [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

check.q: In the radial cross-check, how much time is spent on the attitude indicator?

body.p: Under the view-limiting device, with a safety pilot or instructor watching outside:

bullets: 1. Set cruise power from your POH and put the miniature airplane on the level-flight attitude, wings level [[23:163|IFH 7-2]].
2. Trim until you can let go and it stays put [[23:135|IFH 6-2]] [[24:367|AFH 18-18]].
3. Cross-check: altimeter for pitch, heading indicator for bank, airspeed for power, always coming back to the attitude indicator [[23:170|IFH 7-9]] [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].
4. Altitude off: half a bar under 100 ft, a full bar over 100 ft; VSI about double the error [[23:165|IFH 7-4]] [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].
5. Heading off: bank no more than the degrees to turn, never past standard rate [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].
6. Airspeed off: check altitude first. Fix with pitch, or pitch plus power [[23:169|IFH 7-8]] [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].
7. Keep the ball centered and retrim after every change [[23:169|IFH 7-8]].
8. Keep a light grip and small, smooth inputs [[23:164|IFH 7-3]] [[24:367|AFH 18-18]].

body.p: Tolerances from ACS PA.VIII.A.S2. Cruise power and the level attitude for your airplane come from the POH and your CFI.

callout.text: Fix small errors right away. A 1° error is much easier to fix than a 20° error [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

check.q: What are the ACS limits for this task?
check.a: Altitude ±200 ft, heading ±20°, airspeed ±10 knots (ACS PA.VIII.A.S2).

body.p: From the IFH list of common errors [[23:173|IFH 7-12]] [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]:

head: Area
Error
Fix
rows: Miniature airplane not set for level flight at cruise
Adjust it after the first level-off
Pushing forward for low airspeed when the real cause is low power
Cross-check everything before moving the controls
Small corrections early; tolerated errors grow
Chasing the VSI; making big pitch changes to rush back
Cross-check the altimeter and attitude indicator; small changes
Correcting a 10° error with 20° of bank
Bank no more than the degrees to turn
Correcting the same drift over and over
Look for the cause: often a wing-low trim problem
Abrupt throttle; staring at the power gauge
Small, smooth throttle moves; keep scanning
Using trim instead of control pressure; big trim inputs
Hold attitude first, then trim off pressure in small amounts

callout.text: Fixation: during a heading fix, pilots miss pitch errors. A small power error matters less than a big altitude or heading error [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

check.q: Your heading keeps drifting left no matter how often you correct. What should you look at?
check.a: Trim. A left-wing-low trim problem causes repeated left drift [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

chunks.title: Risk: losing the horizon, disorientation, traffic and getting help

body.p: If you can't control the airplane by the natural horizon, you are in IMC, whatever the weather report says. Treat it as a real emergency [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. First steps: accept it, keep control, get help [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

Without outside cues, your inner ear lies [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]]. It can't sense a roll of 2° per second or less, so you can slide into a bank without feeling it [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. Pulling back in a turn you don't feel tightens the spiral: the graveyard spiral [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

bullets: Believe the instruments, not your body. Keep the wings level first; then pitch control gets easier [[24:367|AFH 18-18]].
Keep head movement small to avoid the coriolis illusion, especially when picking up dropped items [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].
If ATC rushes you, it's fine to ask the controller to slow down [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

Fatigue degrades attention and coordination and narrows your focus to the center of vision [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]. Heavy, ongoing stress makes performance fall off quickly [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. If acutely fatigued, stay on the ground [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]].

body.p: When to ask for help: the moment you're doubtful about position, fuel, weather, or anything else that affects safety, you're in at least an urgency condition. Ask then, not later [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. A non-instrument-rated pilot who can't stay VFR should tell ATC, say they lack an instrument rating, and declare a distress condition [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]. If you can't reach ATC right away, squawk 7700 [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]] [[34:46|AIM 6-3-1]]; if you're already talking to ATC on an assigned code, keep that code unless told otherwise [[34:46|AIM 6-3-1]].

Off-airport option: a precautionary landing is a planned landing, on or off an airport, when you could keep flying but shouldn't; deteriorating weather is one reason. It is less hazardous than a forced landing. A non-instrument-rated pilot trapped by weather who doesn't consider one accepts an extremely hazardous alternative [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

Collision hazards: simulated instrument flight needs a safety pilot with at least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings for the airplane, with good vision forward and to each side [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)]] [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]]. Instructors and safety pilots tend to look inside too much during hood work; they must keep scanning for traffic [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].

check.q: When does the AIM say you're in at least an urgency condition?
check.a: The moment you become doubtful about position, fuel, weather or anything else that could affect safety [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

f4.alt: Turn coordinators and turn-and-slip indicators. Top (skid): left turn with the ball to the right, outside the turn. Bottom (slip): right turn with the ball to the right, inside the turn.

scenario.title: Haze on the way home
scenario.setup: You're a new private pilot flying home late in the afternoon after a long workday. The forecast said VFR, but the haze thickens and the horizon fades into gray. You realize you're glancing between the windshield and the attitude indicator, and the heading has drifted 30° without you noticing. You dropped your pen and reached for it a minute ago.

questions.a: Yes. If you can't keep attitude control by the natural horizon, it counts as IMC whatever the weather is. Treat it as an emergency [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

questions.q: What's wrong with looking outside and inside by turns?
questions.a: Controlling partly by instruments while searching outside gives poor control and can lead to disorientation and loss of control [[24:367|AFH 18-18]]. Commit to the instruments.

questions.q: How did the heading drift without you feeling it?
questions.a: Your inner ear can't sense a roll of 2° per second or less [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. Reaching for the pen added head movement, which can set off the coriolis illusion [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

questions.q: What do you do first with the controls?
questions.a: Wings level on the attitude indicator, light fingertip pressure, pitch changes no more than one bar width, and trim for hands-off level flight [[24:367|AFH 18-18]].

questions.q: Should you call anyone? What do you say?
questions.a: Yes, now. Doubt about the weather already makes it an urgency condition [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. Tell ATC you have no instrument rating and declare distress if you can't stay VFR [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]. Squawk 7700 only if you can't reach ATC right away; if you're already on an assigned code, keep it unless told otherwise [[34:46|AIM 6-3-1]].

questions.q: How did the long workday play into this?
questions.a: Fatigue degrades attention and makes you focus narrowly and miss things in your periphery [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]. That's how fixation and omission creep in [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].

skills.do: Hold straight-and-level flight by instruments alone with a proper cross-check, correct interpretation, and coordinated control.
skills.practice: With your CFI, fly level under a view-limiting device. Call out primary instruments aloud: altimeter, heading, airspeed [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]. Practice the half-bar and full-bar corrections [[23:164|IFH 7-3]].

skills.do: Hold altitude ±200 ft, heading ±20° and airspeed ±10 knots (ACS PA.VIII.A.S2).
skills.practice: Have your CFI give you headings and altitudes, then distract you with radio calls. Fix every error early; don't let small ones grow [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

quiz.q: In this handbook's method, which instrument is primary for pitch in straight-and-level flight?
quiz.why: The IFH normally treats the altimeter as primary for pitch in level flight [[23:167|IFH 7-6]].

quiz.q: You are 80 ft below your altitude. What pitch correction should you start with?
quiz.why: For errors under 100 ft, use a half bar width [[23:165|IFH 7-4]].

quiz.q: You are 100 ft off altitude. About what VSI rate should you use to return?
quiz.why: Use a rate about double the error: 100 ft off means about 200 fpm [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

quiz.q: The static port ices over in level flight. What does the altimeter do?
options: Freezes at the altitude where the port blocked
Acts like an airspeed indicator in the climb
Reads higher and higher until the ice melts
Drops to zero like the vertical speed indicator
quiz.why: Trapped static pressure freezes the altimeter, and the VSI reads zero [[23:98|IFH 5-3]].

quiz.q: You are 10° off heading. What's the most bank you should use?
quiz.why: Bank no more than the number of degrees to turn, and never more than standard rate [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

quiz.q: Airspeed is low and altitude is high. What should you change?
quiz.why: When one is high and the other low, a pitch change alone may fix both [[23:169|IFH 7-8]] [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].

quiz.q: In the radial cross-check, about how much time goes to the attitude indicator?
quiz.why: 80 to 90 percent, with quick glances to the other instruments [[23:144|IFH 6-11]].

quiz.q: A non-instrument-rated pilot can't continue in VFR conditions. What does the AIM say to do?
options: Ask ATC for an instrument approach and fly it yourself
Climb above the clouds and wait for the weather to improve
Turn off the transponder and radios to reduce your workload
Tell ATC you have no instrument rating and declare distress
quiz.why: Advise the controller, say you lack an instrument rating, and declare a distress condition [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].

takeaways: Performance = attitude + power. Set, trim, cross-check, adjust.
Level flight: altimeter for pitch, heading indicator for bank, airspeed for power, and always back to the attitude indicator.
Small corrections: half a bar under 100 ft, a full bar over 100 ft; VSI about double the error.
Know each instrument's errors: gyro precession, heading drift, VSI lag, pitot-static blockage.
Fixation, omission and emphasis are the three scan errors. Keep the eyes moving.
Lost the horizon? Wings level, trust the instruments, and ask for help early.
cfi_notes: Students grip too hard and overcontrol. Have them let go of the yoke briefly when trimmed to feel how stable the airplane is [[23:164|IFH 7-3]].
Have the student say the primary instruments out loud during the first sessions to build the habit.
Demonstrate a large, rushed pitch correction and the resulting overshoot, then the slow, smooth fix [[23:165|IFH 7-4]].
Examiners often probe pitot-static blockage effects and attitude indicator errors; be ready with the table.
As safety pilot, keep your own eyes outside; hood work is when instructors tend to look inside too much [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].
The IFH 7-I examples use a retractable-gear airplane with manifold pressure; translate to the trainer's tachometer and POH numbers.
gaps: Cruise power settings and level-flight pitch attitudes are airplane-specific; use the POH. The IFH examples (e.g., 23 inches MP for 120 knots) are for a sample retractable.
This lesson uses analog instruments. Glass-cockpit (PFD/AHRS) failure modes are in IFH Ch 6-II and 7-II and are not covered here.
Emergency off-airport landings are covered only generically (AFH 18-1). No source gives an instrument-specific off-airport landing procedure for the VFR pilot.

activities.title: Control and performance, step by step
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Set an attitude and power on the control instruments
Trim until the control pressures are gone
If something is off, decide how much and which way to fix it
Adjust the attitude or power on the control instruments

activities.title: True or false: pitch, bank and power

cards.s: You are 60 ft low. Start with a full bar width of nose-up pitch.
cards.why: No. For errors under 100 ft, use a half bar width. A full bar width is for errors over 100 ft [[23:165|IFH 7-4]].

cards.s: To fix a 50 ft altitude error, aim for about 100 fpm on the VSI.
cards.why: Yes. Pick a rate about double the error [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

cards.s: If the heading indicator card is moving fast, the bank is steep.
cards.why: Yes. At the same airspeed, fast card movement means a large bank and slow movement a small one [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

cards.s: To fix a 15° heading error quickly, use about 30° of bank.
cards.why: No. Bank no more than the degrees you need to turn, here 15°, and never more than standard rate [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

cards.s: The ball is right of center. Press right rudder to center it.
cards.why: Yes. Right ball, right rudder. Then level the wings with aileron and retrim [[23:169|IFH 7-8]].

cards.s: Airspeed is low, so add power right away.
cards.why: No. Check the altimeter first. If you are also high, lowering the nose alone may fix both [[23:169|IFH 7-8]] [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].

activities.title: What failed? Match the clue
activities.intro: Tap a problem, then what you would see.

pairs.l: Pitot tube blocked, drain hole open
Pitot tube and drain hole blocked
pairs.r: Airspeed indicator acts like an altimeter
Altimeter freezes and the VSI stays at zero
Altimeter and airspeed read higher than actual

activities.title: Name that scan error
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Staring at an altimeter 200 ft low while the heading slowly wanders
Watching the heading indicator the whole way through a 90° turn
Gazing at the power gauge during a speed change
Rolling out of a turn on the attitude indicator and never checking heading
Leaving an instrument out of the scan after an attitude change
Trying to hold altitude with the attitude indicator alone
Relying on the instrument you understand best, even when it's wrong

final_quiz.q: You are in level cruise in a trainer with a fixed-pitch propeller. Which instrument is primary for power?
final_quiz.why: In straight-and-level flight at constant airspeed, the airspeed indicator is primary for power [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]. The tachometer only supports it [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].

final_quiz.q: The altimeter needle is creeping up and you are now 40 ft high. What is the best technique?
options: Use light pressure to stop the needle, then a small nose-down change
Push the nose down hard to get back to altitude as quickly as possible
Wait; 40 ft is well inside the checkride limits, so just keep watching
Roll in nose-down trim until the needle stops, then hold that trim
final_quiz.why: Correct promptly with light pressure in two steps: stop the needle, then return to altitude [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]. Ignored errors grow, rushed big corrections overcontrol, and trim alone gives erratic control [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

final_quiz.q: You are 250 ft below your altitude. Using the rule of thumb, about what climb rate should you aim for on the VSI?
final_quiz.why: Aim for about double the error, so 250 ft means about 500 fpm, never more than the airplane's best climb rate at that speed [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]. Since the error is over 100 ft, start with a full bar width [[23:165|IFH 7-4]].

final_quiz.q: A distraction leaves you 40° off your heading. What should limit your bank as you turn back?
options: Bank no more than a standard rate turn needs
Bank 40°, one degree for each degree off
Bank at least 45° to fix it fast
Keep the wings level and turn with rudder only
final_quiz.why: Bank no more than the degrees to turn, and never more than standard rate. Bigger banks usually cause overcontrolling [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

final_quiz.q: Your left wing is low and the ball is left of center. How do you fix it?
options: Right rudder to center the ball and left aileron to level the wings
Right rudder only to center the ball, then retrim the airplane
More power to lift the wing, then left aileron to level the wings
Left rudder to center the ball, right aileron to level the wings
final_quiz.why: Step on the ball: left ball, left rudder. Use right aileron to level the wings, then retrim [[23:169|IFH 7-8]].

final_quiz.q: You are 100 ft above your altitude and 10 knots faster than your planned cruise speed. What fixes both?
options: Lower the nose and reduce power
Raise the nose and add power
final_quiz.why: When altitude and airspeed are both high, you need a change in both pitch and power: lower the nose and reduce power [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].

final_quiz.q: You set the heading indicator to the magnetic compass before takeoff and haven't touched it in the hour since. What is true?
options: It is still exact, because the gyro stays rigid in space
It may have drifted; compare it with the compass and reset
It has tumbled in the hour and must be caged before use
It now points to true north instead of magnetic north
final_quiz.why: A heading indicator is not north-seeking. Earth's rotation makes it drift about 15° per hour, so check it against the compass at least every 15 minutes [[23:115|IFH 5-20]].

final_quiz.q: Your static port ices over at 6,000 ft. The pitot tube stays clear and you descend to 4,000 ft. What does the airspeed indicator show?
final_quiz.why: Below the altitude where the static port blocked, the trapped low pressure makes airspeed read high. Above it, airspeed reads low [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]. The altimeter stays frozen at 6,000 ft.

final_quiz.q: On your checkride you are assigned 3,500 ft, heading 270° and 100 knots. Which reading is outside the ACS limits?
final_quiz.why: Heading 292° is 22° off, past the ±20° limit. The others are inside ±200 ft and ±10 knots (ACS PA.VIII.A.S2). Fix small errors early so they never get that big [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

final_quiz.q: In the clouds, the airplane slowly rolls into a bank at about 1° per second. What will your inner ear most likely sense?
options: A feeling of rolling the opposite way at once
Nothing; the roll is too slow to feel
final_quiz.why: Rotation of 2° per second or less is below what the inner ear can detect [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. That is why you must trust the instruments.

final_quiz.q: You fly into a cloud by mistake. Once you accept the situation, what does the AFH call your most important concern?
options: Looking outside for a break to confirm the instruments
Making a steep turn back right away
final_quiz.why: The most important concern at this point is to keep the wings level; good bank control makes pitch control much easier. Searching outside while flying on instruments leads to poor control [[24:367|AFH 18-18]].

final_quiz.q: Ceilings are lowering ahead and you are not sure you can stay VFR. When does the AIM say to ask ATC for help?
options: Only after you are inside a cloud and cannot see the ground
Only after you have declared a distress condition on 121.5
Right now, since weather doubt is already an urgency condition
After trying to find your own way for about 10 minutes more
final_quiz.why: You are in at least an urgency condition the moment you doubt the weather. That is the time to ask for help, not later [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

final_quiz.q: You plan hood practice in a Cessna 172 with a friend as safety pilot. Who meets 14 CFR 91.109(c)?
options: A student pilot with 30 hours who has an airplane solo endorsement
A private pilot rated in airplanes who sees well forward and to each side
Any passenger who promises to watch for traffic and has good eyesight
A private pilot rated only for helicopters who sees well in all directions
final_quiz.why: The safety pilot needs at least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings for the airplane [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]], and adequate vision forward and to each side [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]].
